questions.question: [JavaScript • Test 1 • Q1] What is the result of evaluating the logical nullish assignment operator expression 'obj.x ??= 10;' given the object initialization 'const obj = { x: null };'?
options: null
undefined
TypeError
questions.explanation: The nullish coalescing assignment operator (??=) evaluates the right-hand side and assigns it to the left-hand side only if the left-hand side evaluates to null or undefined. Since obj.x is null, 10 is assigned.
questions.hint: Think about which falsy values trigger the nullish assignment versus regular logical assignment (||=).
questions.relatedConcept: Nullish coalescing assignment (??=) and short-circuiting semantics
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to check if candidates know the modern ES2021 assignment operators and how they differ specifically from the traditional OR assignment operator (||=) regarding values like 0, false, and empty strings.

questions.question: [JavaScript • Test 1 • Q2] Which of the following describes the execution and lookup behavior of class field declarations using private identifiers (prefixed with '#') in JavaScript classes?
options: Private identifiers are merely a syntactic naming convention and compile down to standard properties with weak map lookups, meaning they can be accessed externally if the property name string is known.
Private fields are hoisted to the top of the enclosing scope and can be referenced inside static methods without an explicit class instance.

Private identifiers are strictly enforced at the syntax and runtime level by the engine using hard encapsulation, and attempting to access '#count' outside the class throws a SyntaxError or TypeError depending on context.
Private identifiers are shared across all instances of subclasses, acting as protected members in traditional object-oriented languages.
questions.correctAnswer: Private identifiers are strictly enforced at the syntax and runtime level by the engine using hard encapsulation, and attempting to access '#count' outside the class throws a SyntaxError or TypeError depending on context.
questions.explanation: Private identifiers (#) provide hard runtime encapsulation built into the language specification. Accessing a private field from outside its defining class body results in a syntax or type error, preventing external tampering.
questions.hint: Consider whether JavaScript private fields are merely convention-based or hard-enforced by the parsing and runtime engines.
questions.relatedConcept: ESNext private class features and encapsulation
questions.interviewTip: Senior JavaScript interviewers love asking about class fields to verify whether developers understand native private syntax versus legacy closure or WeakMap encapsulation patterns.

questions.question: [JavaScript • Test 1 • Q3] What is the exact behavior of JavaScript's `Object.freeze()` when applied to an object that contains nested property objects?
options: It throws a TypeError in strict mode when attempting to modify nested properties.
It makes the object and all its nested properties completely immutable recursively.
It silents the modification and reverts the nested property back to its initial value.
It only freezes the top-level properties; nested objects remain mutable unless explicitly frozen separately.
questions.correctAnswer: It only freezes the top-level properties; nested objects remain mutable unless explicitly frozen separately.
questions.explanation: Object.freeze() is shallow. It only freezes the immediate properties of the target object. Nested objects are not frozen automatically and can still be modified unless Object.freeze() is called on them individually.
questions.hint: Think about whether immutability spreads recursively down the object tree by default in JavaScript.
questions.relatedConcept: Object.freeze() shallow immutability and nested object mutation
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to test if candidates understand the limitation of built-in shallow freezing vs deep immutability.

questions.question: [JavaScript • Test 1 • Q4] What is the output or behavior of calling a generator function after it has already completed (i.e., its return value has been reached or it has thrown an unhandled exception)?
options: It returns an object `{ value: undefined, done: true }` indefinitely on subsequent calls.
It throws a Runtime ReferenceError because the generator execution context is destroyed.
It restarts the generator execution from the beginning.
It returns `{ value: 2, done: false }` repeatedly.
questions.correctAnswer: It returns an object `{ value: undefined, done: true }` indefinitely on subsequent calls.
questions.explanation: Once a generator completes (done: true), any subsequent calls to .next() will continue to return { value: undefined, done: true } and will not re-execute or throw errors.
questions.hint: Consider the state and shape of the iterator result object once a generator finishes.
questions.relatedConcept: JavaScript Generator iterator completion behavior
questions.interviewTip: Useful for checking deep knowledge of iterators, generators, and state management in modern JavaScript.

questions.question: [JavaScript • Test 1 • Q5] What is the structural performance limitation of V8 Hidden Classes (Shapes) when adding properties to an object out-of-order across multiple instances?
options: It causes v1 and p1 to transition to dictionary mode, completely bypassing optimized inline cache lookups.
It creates distinct hidden class transition chains, preventing the engine from sharing property offset maps and forcing slow-path lookups.
It triggers an immediate V8 garbage collection cycle to compact the object memory heap.
It automatically sorts the internal property keys alphabetically to maintain constant-time property access.
questions.correctAnswer: It creates distinct hidden class transition chains, preventing the engine from sharing property offset maps and forcing slow-path lookups.
questions.explanation: V8 constructs hidden classes (shapes) based on the exact sequence in which properties are added. Because p1 adds 'z' after 'y', while Vector adds 'z' before 'y', they diverge into different transition trees. This prevents monomorphic inline caches from optimizing property access across these instances.
questions.hint: Think about how property assignment order affects hidden class transition trees in modern JS engines.
questions.relatedConcept: V8 hidden classes and shape transitions
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to test if candidates understand how object property initialization order impacts JavaScript engine optimization.

questions.question: [JavaScript • Test 1 • Q6] How does the V8 engine handle elements backing stores when sparse array operations introduce a massive non-consecutive index?
options: It allocates a contiguous dense buffer padded with null values for all intervening indices to ensure uniform $O(1)$ memory offset calculation.
It throws an out-of-memory exception because array indices must always fit within contiguous memory blocks.
It transitions the array storage from a contiguous elements backing store to a dictionary-based (hash table) backing store.
It truncates the array length to prevent memory bloat and ignores indices greater than 10,000.
questions.correctAnswer: It transitions the array storage from a contiguous elements backing store to a dictionary-based (hash table) backing store.
questions.explanation: When an array becomes sparse with a huge gap, maintaining a contiguous allocation would waste massive amounts of RAM. V8 automatically converts the internal elements representation from a dense array (PACKED_ELEMENTS or HOLEY_ELEMENTS) to a dictionary (hash table) to save memory, at the cost of slower index access times.
questions.hint: Consider the memory overhead of allocating a million empty slots in a contiguous layout.
questions.relatedConcept: JavaScript sparse array internal representation
questions.interviewTip: Great for assessing deep understanding of V8 memory management internals and array performance characteristics.

questions.question: [JavaScript • Test 1 • Q7] What is the primary mechanism that enables JavaScript generator functions (`function*`) to suspend execution and resume later while maintaining their local state?
options: The JavaScript engine allocates a separate dedicated thread for each generator instance, pausing and unblocking the thread via OS-level primitives.
The execution stack frame is copied directly into the heap on every yield statement and restored upon calling next().
Generators rely on asynchronous Web Workers running in the background to handle paused states asynchronously.
The compiler transforms the generator into a state machine object where local variables and execution position are captured across iterator calls.
questions.correctAnswer: The compiler transforms the generator into a state machine object where local variables and execution position are captured across iterator calls.
questions.explanation: Generators are implemented under the hood as state machines. When a generator yields, the JavaScript engine stores the local execution context and current pointer state inside a generator object on the heap, avoiding heavy OS thread manipulation or full stack frame copying.
questions.hint: Think about how JavaScript's single-threaded event loop can pause execution without blocking worker threads.
questions.relatedConcept: JavaScript Generators and State Machine Transformations
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to test your understanding of language abstractions versus underlying engine mechanics (V8/SpiderMonkey).

questions.question: [JavaScript • Test 1 • Q8] In modern JavaScript, what happens when you attempt to use a `WeakMap` with primitive values (such as strings or numbers) as keys?
questions.codeSnippet:
const wm = new WeakMap();
wm.set("keyStr", "value");
options: A TypeError is thrown because WeakMap keys must be objects or non-registered symbols.
The primitive is automatically boxed into an object wrapper (e.g., String object) before being stored as a valid key.
The primitive is stored successfully, but it is immediately eligible for garbage collection.
The primitive acts as a global shared reference key similar to string interning in traditional languages.
questions.correctAnswer: A TypeError is thrown because WeakMap keys must be objects or non-registered symbols.
questions.explanation: WeakMap keys must be garbage-collectable, which in JavaScript applies exclusively to objects and non-registered symbols. Primitives (like strings, numbers, booleans) cannot be garbage collected independently of their value representation, so passing them as a WeakMap key throws a TypeError.
questions.hint: Recall the strict type constraints imposed by weak collection references regarding garbage collection.
questions.relatedConcept: WeakMap Constraints and Garbage Collection
questions.interviewTip: A classic trap question to check if the candidate truly understands memory management and garbage collection requirements in JavaScript collections.

questions.question: [JavaScript • Test 1 • Q9] What is the primary mechanism by which WeakRef and FinalizationRegistry in modern JavaScript interact with the garbage collector?
options: FinalizationRegistry callbacks execute synchronously on the exact main thread cycle that the object reference count drops to zero.
FinalizationRegistry callbacks are executed asynchronously at an indeterminate time after the target object is garbage collected, and do not guarantee immediate execution.
WeakRef prevents an object from being garbage collected until deref() is explicitly invoked to release it.
WeakRef automatically triggers a synchronous garbage collection pass when the referenced object goes out of scope.
questions.correctAnswer: FinalizationRegistry callbacks are executed asynchronously at an indeterminate time after the target object is garbage collected, and do not guarantee immediate execution.
questions.explanation: WeakRef allows holding a weak reference to an object without preventing its collection. FinalizationRegistry allows cleaning up tasks when an object is garbage-collected, but browser or engine vendors execute these cleanup callbacks asynchronously and non-deterministically to avoid exposing internal garbage collection schedules or locking the event loop.
questions.hint: Consider whether garbage collection hooks in JS are deterministic or synchronous.
questions.relatedConcept: Garbage Collection, WeakRef, and FinalizationRegistry behavior
questions.interviewTip: Intermediary to advanced interviewers use this to test your understanding of JS runtime memory management and the intentional non-determinism of engine-level GC hooks.

questions.question: [JavaScript • Test 1 • Q10] When dealing with Web Workers in the browser, how are ArrayBuffer objects transferred from the main thread to a worker, and what is the consequence on the source buffer?
options: The ArrayBuffer is deeply cloned across threads, preserving the original buffer intact on the main thread with its full byteLength.
The ArrayBuffer is shared via underlying SharedArrayBuffer mechanics, keeping both threads able to read and write to the same memory block simultaneously.
The ArrayBuffer is transferrable; ownership is transferred to the worker via zero-copy operations, leaving the source buffer detached with a byteLength of 0.
The operation throws a DataCloneError because ArrayBuffer cannot cross thread boundaries without explicit JSON serialization.
questions.correctAnswer: The ArrayBuffer is transferrable; ownership is transferred to the worker via zero-copy operations, leaving the source buffer detached with a byteLength of 0.
questions.explanation: Passing an ArrayBuffer in the transfer list of postMessage transfers ownership of the memory space to the receiving context (the worker). This is a high-performance zero-copy operation, but it renders the original buffer in the sender context 'detached', meaning its byteLength becomes 0 and it can no longer be accessed.
questions.hint: Think about what happens to the second argument array (the transfer list) when passing binary data to a worker.
questions.relatedConcept: Web Workers, Transferable Objects, and ArrayBuffer detachment
questions.interviewTip: Critical for high-performance frontend engineering roles where large data payloads or WebAssembly memory buffers are passed between threads.

questions.question: [JavaScript • Test 1 • Q11] What is the exact execution order and output sequence when handling microtasks and macrotasks in the JavaScript event loop with the following asynchronous code snippet?
options: A, E, B, C, D
A, C, E, B, D
A, E, C, D, B
A, E, C, B, D
questions.correctAnswer: A, E, C, B, D
questions.explanation: Synchronous statements execute first ('A', then 'E'). Next, the microtask queue is drained completely, running the Promise then-callback ('C'). During this microtask execution, a new macrotask 'D' is scheduled via setTimeout. Once the microtask queue is empty, the event loop picks up the earliest macrotasks in FIFO order: first the initial setTimeout callback ('B'), then the newly scheduled one ('D'). Thus, the sequence is A, E, C, B, D.
questions.hint: Remember that all pending microtasks run immediately after the current call stack clears, before any macrotask from the task queue.
questions.relatedConcept: JavaScript Event Loop, Microtask Queue vs Macrotask Queue execution order
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to test if candidates understand that microtasks completely drain before moving to the next macrotask, and that microtasks can themselves enqueue new macrotasks.

questions.question: [JavaScript • Test 1 • Q12] In JavaScript, how does the V8 engine handle hidden classes (Maps) and inline caching when object property assignment occurs dynamically outside the constructor?
options: p2 transitions to a different hidden class than p1, which can degrade property access optimization (deoptimization or megamorphic state) for functions expecting uniform shapes.
p2 retains the exact same hidden class as p1 because hidden classes only track method definitions, not instance properties.
p2's hidden class is unaffected because dynamic property addition is optimized inline without creating new transitions.
p1 and p2 both share a single dictionary mode structure from the start, bypassing hidden classes entirely.
questions.correctAnswer: p2 transitions to a different hidden class than p1, which can degrade property access optimization (deoptimization or megamorphic state) for functions expecting uniform shapes.
questions.explanation: Adding a property 'z' dynamically to 'p2' causes it to transition to a new hidden class (shape) that differs from 'p1'. If functions are called with objects of varying hidden classes, inline caching can fall back to a megamorphic state, reducing execution performance.
questions.hint: Consider how adding a property alters the internal shape transition path of an instantiated object.
questions.relatedConcept: V8 Hidden Classes, Shapes, and Inline Caching
questions.interviewTip: This tests deep knowledge of JavaScript engine internals and why consistent object shape initialization matters for performance.

questions.question: [JavaScript • Test 1 • Q13] What does a TypeError stating 'Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'toString')' at runtime typically diagnose in a JavaScript application?
questions.codeSnippet:
const user = fetchUser();
console.log(user.profile.toString());
options: The JavaScript engine ran out of heap memory while trying to allocate string conversion prototypes
An asynchronous operation returned undefined because it was not awaited or resolved before property access
The strict mode parser encountered an invalid variable identifier declaration during hoisting
The V8 compiler optimized out the method call due to a missing type signature annotation
questions.correctAnswer: An asynchronous operation returned undefined because it was not awaited or resolved before property access
questions.explanation: This specific TypeError occurs when you attempt to access a property or method on a value that evaluates to undefined. In modern asynchronous JavaScript, attempting to call a method like toString() on the result of an un-awaited fetch or an asynchronous lookup that hasn't returned its payload yet will evaluate to undefined, triggering this runtime crash.
questions.hint: Think about what happens when you chain property lookups on the return value of an un-awaited asynchronous function.
questions.relatedConcept: Asynchronous runtime behavior and null/undefined reference debugging
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to test if candidates can link a common runtime exception message directly to asynchronous flow control mistakes.

questions.question: [JavaScript • Test 1 • Q14] Why does modifying a property on a deeply nested object inside a React state updater occasionally fail to trigger a UI re-render, despite the mutation executing without throwing an error?
options: JavaScript objects use internal proxies that throw security exceptions when mutated outside of defined setter descriptors
React state properties are automatically frozen with Object.freeze() upon initial component mount
State reconciliation relies on reference equality checks; mutating the nested object in place leaves the top-level reference identical, so React skips rendering
The V8 engine garbage collects unassigned object branches before the virtual DOM can detect changes
questions.correctAnswer: State reconciliation relies on reference equality checks; mutating the nested object in place leaves the top-level reference identical, so React skips rendering
questions.explanation: React hooks determine whether a re-render is necessary by performing a shallow reference comparison (Object.is) on the state value passed to setState. Because state.user.name = 'Bob' mutates the existing object in place without changing its memory reference, passing 'state' back into setState causes React to conclude that nothing changed, bypassing the re-render cycle.
questions.hint: Consider how React checks whether state has changed when setState is invoked.
questions.relatedConcept: Immutability requirements in state management and reference equality
questions.interviewTip: This is a classic debugging scenario that separates junior developers who mutate state directly from senior developers who understand reference immutability.

questions.question: [JavaScript • Test 1 • Q15] What is the exact result and behavior when evaluating the expression `Number(null)` versus `Number(undefined)` in JavaScript?
questions.codeSnippet:
console.log(Number(null));
console.log(Number(undefined));
options: NaN and 0 respectively
0 and 0 respectively
NaN and NaN respectively
0 and NaN respectively
questions.correctAnswer: 0 and NaN respectively
questions.explanation: In JavaScript's type coercion rules, `null` is explicitly converted to the numeric value `0` when passed through the `Number()` constructor (or unary plus operator), whereas `undefined` lacks a meaningful numeric representation and converts to `NaN` (Not-a-Number).
questions.hint: Think about how JavaScript treats intentional absence of value versus uninitialized variables during explicit type conversion.
questions.relatedConcept: JavaScript explicit type conversion and coercion rules for primitive null/undefined values
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to test whether a candidate understands the precise edge cases of JavaScript type casting rather than relying on loose falsy assumptions.

questions.question: [JavaScript • Test 1 • Q16] How does the JavaScript `Intl.Collator` API handle string comparisons when options are left at their default settings, compared to standard lexicographical operators like `<` or `>`?
options: Intl.Collator is locale-sensitive and case-insensitive by default (returns 0 for 'a' and 'A'), whereas standard operators perform strict code-point comparisons ('a' < 'A' is false because 97 < 65 is false).
Intl.Collator performs strict Unicode code-point comparison just like standard operators, but returns numbers (-1, 0, 1) instead of booleans.
Intl.Collator is case-sensitive by default, but standard operators ignore case differences automatically.
Intl.Collator automatically normalizes accents and case differences, whereas standard operators throw a TypeError on accented characters.
questions.correctAnswer: Intl.Collator is locale-sensitive and case-insensitive by default (returns 0 for 'a' and 'A'), whereas standard operators perform strict code-point comparisons ('a' < 'A' is false because 97 < 65 is false).
questions.explanation: By default, `Intl.Collator` uses the default locale and is sensitive to language-specific sorting rules where case variants can be treated as equivalent or sorted according to locale collation specifications, whereas standard comparison operators (`<`, `>`, `===`) compare raw UTF-16 code units directly (where 'a' is 97 and 'A' is 65, making 'a' < 'A' evaluate to false).
questions.hint: Examine the ASCII/Unicode values involved in string comparisons versus locale-aware sorting utilities.
questions.relatedConcept: Intl.Collator locale-sensitive string comparison versus operator-based Unicode code-point comparison
questions.interviewTip: This question assesses whether the candidate knows built-in internationalization tools and how they differ fundamentally from primitive language operators.

questions.question: [JavaScript • Test 1 • Q17] What is the precise execution behavior of JavaScript's `String.prototype.replaceAll()` when the search value is an empty string `""`?
questions.codeSnippet: console.log("abc".replaceAll("", "-"));
options: It throws a TypeError because an empty search string is disallowed in replaceAll.
It inserts the replacement string between every character, at the start, and at the end of the string (e.g., "-a-b-c-").
It returns the original string unmodified since an empty search string has no matching length.
It replaces only the very first character of the string with the replacement.
questions.correctAnswer: It inserts the replacement string between every character, at the start, and at the end of the string (e.g., "-a-b-c-").
questions.explanation: According to the ECMAScript specification for String.prototype.replaceAll, when searching for an empty string, it matches the empty positions between every adjacent pair of characters as well as the start and end of the string, resulting in the replacement string being interleaved.
questions.hint: Think about what an empty string matches in terms of boundary positions across the entire target string.
questions.relatedConcept: JavaScript String.prototype.replaceAll empty string edge case semantics
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to test whether candidates deeply read specifications or rely solely on intuitive assumptions about string manipulation methods.

questions.question: [JavaScript • Test 1 • Q18] In JavaScript, how does the `Array.prototype.sort()` specification handle comparison functions that violate transitive consistency (i.e., when `compare(a, b)` and `compare(b, c)` do not correctly imply the relationship for `compare(a, c)`)?
questions.codeSnippet:
const arr = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9];
arr.sort((a, b) => (Math.random() > 0.5 ? 1 : -1));
options: The V8 engine automatically catches the violation, throws a TypeError, and halts execution.
The engine falls back to a deterministic Insertion Sort to guarantee strict mathematical ordering.
The specification does not mandate a specific sorting algorithm or error, meaning the resulting sort order, stability, and browser behavior are undefined or implementation-dependent.
The array is left completely untouched and returns a reference to the original unsorted array.
questions.correctAnswer: The specification does not mandate a specific sorting algorithm or error, meaning the resulting sort order, stability, and browser behavior are undefined or implementation-dependent.
questions.explanation: The ECMAScript standard does not enforce a specific sorting algorithm (though Timsort or Quicksort variants are common), and if a comparator function is not a consistent equivalence relation or lacks transitivity, the resulting behavior is completely implementation-dependent and can lead to corrupted or erratic sorting.
questions.hint: Consider whether JavaScript engines enforce strict mathematical rules at runtime for user-supplied comparison callbacks.
questions.relatedConcept: Array.prototype.sort comparator function stability and transitivity violations
questions.interviewTip: This tests advanced knowledge of language standards, runtime guarantees, and the subtle pitfalls of non-pure or non-transitive comparator callbacks.

questions.question: [JavaScript • Test 1 • Q19] What is the result of evaluating the conditional operator expression `false ? 'a' : true ? 'b' : 'c'` in JavaScript?
questions.codeSnippet:
const result = false ? 'a' : true ? 'b' : 'c';
console.log(result);
options: SyntaxError
questions.explanation: The conditional (ternary) operator evaluates right-to-left due to its associativity, or rather, it is parsed such that `false ? 'a' : (true ? 'b' : 'c')`. Since the first condition `false` is falsy, it evaluates the alternative branch `true ? 'b' : 'c'`, which then evaluates to `'b'` because its condition `true` is truthy.
questions.hint: Check the associativity and grouping order of nested ternary operators in JavaScript.
questions.relatedConcept: Ternary operator associativity and evaluation precedence
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use nested ternaries to test whether candidates understand JavaScript operator precedence and associativity rules.

questions.question: [JavaScript • Test 1 • Q20] What happens when you attempt to use the `delete` operator on a configurable property versus a non-configurable property created via `Object.defineProperty` in strict mode?
options: It throws a TypeError in strict mode.
It successfully deletes the property and returns true.
It silently fails and returns false without throwing an error.
It removes the value but keeps the property key with an undefined value.
questions.correctAnswer: It throws a TypeError in strict mode.
questions.explanation: In strict mode, attempting to delete a non-configurable property explicitly throws a TypeError. In non-strict mode, it would fail silently and return false.
questions.hint: Consider the behavior of strict mode when an operation is invalid or forbidden on property descriptors.
questions.relatedConcept: Strict mode behavior with non-configurable property deletion
questions.interviewTip: This tests knowledge of JavaScript property attributes, strict mode semantics, and error handling for invalid operations.

questions.question: [JavaScript • Test 1 • Q21] What is the primary performance and memory implication of invoking Array.prototype.flat() on a deeply nested sparse array in V8-based JavaScript engines?
options: It preserves empty slots as sparse holes, dropping memory consumption significantly while retaining index properties.
It converts empty slots into explicit 'undefined' elements, turning a sparse array into a dense array and potentially causing massive memory reallocation and performance overhead.
It throws a RangeError due to stack overflow caused by internal recursive flattening of sparse structures.
It automatically optimizes to a TypedArray under the hood to handle deep nesting without memory expansion.
questions.correctAnswer: It converts empty slots into explicit 'undefined' elements, turning a sparse array into a dense array and potentially causing massive memory reallocation and performance overhead.
questions.explanation: Array.prototype.flat() and flatMap() do not preserve sparseness; they collapse empty slots and treat them as undefined values when flattening. This transforms a highly memory-efficient sparse array into a dense array filled with 'undefined' entries, triggering substantial memory allocation and garbage collection pressure.
questions.hint: Think about how standard built-in higher-order array methods deal with missing indices versus explicitly assigned values.
questions.relatedConcept: JavaScript sparse array densification and memory overhead via Array.prototype.flat
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to test your understanding of how high-level built-in methods interact with internal engine representations like sparseness and density.

questions.question: [JavaScript • Test 1 • Q22] When measuring the execution time of code blocks using console.time() versus performance.now(), what is the primary architectural reason performance.now() is preferred for high-precision benchmarking in modern JavaScript environments?
options: console.time() executes synchronously on the main thread blocking all layout passes, while performance.now() runs entirely on a separate background worker thread.
performance.now() automatically normalizes JIT compilation warmup phases, while console.time() measures cold execution times exclusively.

performance.now() returns a floating-point number with microsecond precision tied to a monotonic clock unaffected by system clock adjustments, whereas console.time() relies on wall-clock time with coarse granularity and console I/O latency interference.
console.time() uses performance.now() internally but introduces artificial jitter by hashing the resulting timestamps for security reasons.
questions.correctAnswer: performance.now() returns a floating-point number with microsecond precision tied to a monotonic clock unaffected by system clock adjustments, whereas console.time() relies on wall-clock time with coarse granularity and console I/O latency interference.
questions.explanation: console.time relies on system wall-clock time, which can be modified by NTP syncs, and its output is subject to asynchronous console I/O overhead. performance.now() provides a high-resolution monotonic timestamp measured in milliseconds with sub-millisecond precision that is immune to system clock skews.
questions.hint: Consider the difference between monotonic clocks and wall-clock time, as well as the side-effects of I/O operations.
questions.relatedConcept: High-precision performance measurement, monotonic clocks, and I/O interference in JavaScript benchmarks
questions.interviewTip: Great for assessing whether a candidate understands practical frontend/Node.js profiling limitations and accurate performance tracking.

questions.question: [JavaScript • Test 1 • Q23] What is the primary operational difference between using 'Array.prototype.sort()' directly on an array of numbers versus providing a custom comparator function?
questions.codeSnippet:
const nums = [10, 5, 20, 15];
nums.sort();
options: Without a comparator, JavaScript sorts elements using an unstable numerical sort algorithm.
Without a comparator, JavaScript throws a TypeError because numbers lack a default ordering.
Without a comparator, the array is sorted in descending order by default instead of ascending.
Without a comparator, elements are converted to strings and compared lexicographically, meaning 10 comes before 2.
questions.correctAnswer: Without a comparator, elements are converted to strings and compared lexicographically, meaning 10 comes before 2.
questions.explanation: By default, the JavaScript sort method converts all elements to strings and compares their UTF-16 code unit values. Consequently, '10' precedes '2' because '1' comes before '2' lexicographically, which frequently causes subtle bugs when sorting numbers.
questions.hint: Think about how JavaScript treats array elements when no sorting function is supplied.
questions.relatedConcept: Array.prototype.sort default lexicographical conversion
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers often look for candidates who catch this implicit type conversion pitfall when reviewing code that sorts numeric data.

questions.question: [JavaScript • Test 1 • Q24] What is the key behavioral characteristic of JavaScript's 'Intl.Collator' when compared to standard string comparison operators like '<' and '>'?
questions.codeSnippet:
const collator = new Intl.Collator('de', { sensitivity: 'accent' });
console.log(collator.compare('ä', 'z'));
options: It provides language-sensitive string comparison, respecting locale-specific collation rules and handling diacritics correctly.
It performs case-insensitive comparisons exclusively and cannot be configured for locale rules.
It converts strings into numeric hash values prior to comparison for optimized performance.
It is strictly designed for sorting currency strings and throws an error for regular alphabetical text.
questions.correctAnswer: It provides language-sensitive string comparison, respecting locale-specific collation rules and handling diacritics correctly.
questions.explanation: Intl.Collator enables language-sensitive string comparison, ensuring that alphabets and diacritics from different locales are sorted correctly according to regional rules, unlike standard relational operators which rely purely on UTF-16 code point values.
questions.hint: Consider how internationalization affects character sorting and string ordering across different languages.
questions.relatedConcept: Intl.Collator locale-aware comparison
questions.interviewTip: Useful for assessing a candidate's awareness of internationalization requirements in modern web applications.

questions.question: [JavaScript • Test 1 • Q25] What happens to the underlying memory buffer of a TypedArray (such as Float64Array) after it is detached and transferred to a Web Worker using structured cloning with transferables?
options: The view remains accessible and `byteLength` prints 64, but reading or writing throws a TypeError.
The underlying buffer is detached, making its byteLength 0, and the associated TypedArray view's byteLength also becomes 0.
The view is completely garbage collected immediately, throwing a ReferenceError upon access.
The view retains its reference and continues to read unmanaged memory safely.
questions.correctAnswer: The underlying buffer is detached, making its byteLength 0, and the associated TypedArray view's byteLength also becomes 0.
questions.explanation: When an ArrayBuffer is transferred to a Web Worker, it becomes detached in the sending context. Its byteLength becomes 0, and any TypedArray views attached to that buffer also become detached, reporting a byteLength of 0.
questions.hint: Consider the state of an ArrayBuffer and its views after ownership transfer.
questions.relatedConcept: Web Workers, Transferable Objects, and ArrayBuffer detachment semantics
questions.interviewTip: Tests deep understanding of low-level memory ownership transfer and thread safety in modern browser APIs.

questions.question: [JavaScript • Test 1 • Q26] How does V8's optimization pipeline handle prototype property additions to an existing constructor function after instances have already been instantiated?
options: Both p1 and p2 transition to a new hidden class because adding a property to the prototype invalidates all existing object shapes.
p1 retains its original hidden class while p2 receives a newly transitioned hidden class that incorporates the prototype change lookup.
Both p1 and p2 retain their original hidden class shapes, but property lookup on the prototype chain dynamically adjusts without mutating the instance shapes.
Instance creation for p2 forces V8 to rebuild the constructor's initial map from scratch, resetting p1's inline caches.
questions.correctAnswer: Both p1 and p2 retain their original hidden class shapes, but property lookup on the prototype chain dynamically adjusts without mutating the instance shapes.
questions.explanation: Hidden classes (maps) track the structure of individual instances, not the prototype object. Adding properties to a constructor's `.prototype` object does not mutate the hidden class of existing or new instances; rather, prototype chain lookup handles the resolution at runtime.
questions.hint: Recall that hidden classes track own-properties of instances, while prototypes exist higher up the lookup chain.
questions.relatedConcept: V8 Hidden Classes, Prototype Chains, and Shape Stability
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to probe engine internals regarding object layout optimization versus dynamic inheritance.

questions.question: [JavaScript • Test 1 • Q27] What is the exact execution order and output of the following asynchronous JavaScript program utilizing Promises, `setTimeout`, and `queueMicrotask`?
options: A, F, C, D, E, B
A, F, E, C, D, B
A, B, C, D, E, F
A, F, C, E, D, B
questions.correctAnswer: A, F, C, E, D, B
questions.explanation: Synchronous code runs first ('A', 'F'). Then, all microtasks queued during synchronous execution run in FIFO order: the Promise chain ('C') and the initial `queueMicrotask` ('E'). Since 'C' executes a nested `queueMicrotask`, 'D' is added to the end of the current microtask queue and runs immediately after 'C' and 'E' finish. Finally, macrotasks like `setTimeout` run ('B'). Thus, the exact order is A, F, C, E, D, B.
questions.hint: Track synchronous logs first, then all microtasks (including nested microtasks spawned before the queue clears) before any macrotask runs.
questions.relatedConcept: JavaScript Event Loop microtask queue draining behavior with nested microtasks
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use microtask nesting scenarios to check if candidates understand that microtasks scheduled within a microtask run in the same tick before yielding back to the macrotask queue.

questions.question: [JavaScript • Test 1 • Q28] How does JavaScript's `Proxy` handle trap invariants when attempting to define a non-configurable property on a target object?
options: It throws a TypeError because the target object does not yet reflect the non-configurable property state when the trap returns.
It successfully defines the property and returns the proxy object.
It silently ignores the definition because proxies cannot handle non-configurable descriptors.
It throws a TypeError because the trap returned `true` instead of returning the descriptor object itself.
questions.correctAnswer: It throws a TypeError because the target object does not yet reflect the non-configurable property state when the trap returns.
questions.explanation: Proxy invariants enforce that a property cannot be reported as non-configurable by the `defineProperty` trap if it does not already exist as a non-configurable property on the target object, or if the target object's state hasn't been updated to match prior to returning true. Specifically, if the target is extensible or lacks the non-configurable descriptor, the ECMAScript engine throws a TypeError to maintain structural integrity.
questions.hint: Proxies enforce strict invariants regarding property configurability and extensibility matching between the trap return value and the actual target state.
questions.relatedConcept: Proxy trap invariants and target property descriptor synchronization
questions.interviewTip: Advanced JavaScript interviews test Proxy invariants to see if candidates know that metadata restrictions exist to prevent illusions about object underlying states.

questions.question: [JavaScript • Test 1 • Q29] What is the primary implication when JavaScript proxy traps for 'get' and 'set' fail to intercept property modifications made via 'Object.defineProperty(target, prop, descriptor)' on the target object?
options: Object.defineProperty cannot be trapped by ECMAScript Proxies by design due to security restrictions in the V8 engine.
Direct operations on the underlying target object bypass the proxy instance entirely, as the proxy only intercepts operations performed directly through the proxy reference.
The descriptor lacks 'configurable: true', which prevents proxy interception of the property definition.
Reflect.set must be called with a receiver argument matching the target rather than the proxy to catch defineProperty hooks.
questions.correctAnswer: Direct operations on the underlying target object bypass the proxy instance entirely, as the proxy only intercepts operations performed directly through the proxy reference.
questions.explanation: Proxies wrap a target object and only intercept operations performed on the proxy object itself. Modifying the target object directly bypasses all proxy traps because no operation is dispatched through the proxy handler.
questions.hint: Consider which object is being operated on: the proxy wrapper or the raw target.
questions.relatedConcept: JavaScript Proxies and Target Object Transparency
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to test whether a candidate understands that Proxies are wrappers rather than universal object monitors.

questions.question: [JavaScript • Test 1 • Q30] What does a sudden, significant increase in V8 major mark-compact garbage collection pauses accompanied by stable heap usage typically indicate about the application's memory lifecycle?
options: An unbounded memory leak in global variables causing the heap size limit to be continuously reached.
Excessive string intercision causing the string table to trigger compaction cycles.
High rates of object promotion from the young generation to the old generation due to medium-lived objects surviving multiple minor GCs.
A sudden drop in available system RAM forcing the V8 engine to offload pages to virtual memory.
questions.correctAnswer: High rates of object promotion from the young generation to the old generation due to medium-lived objects surviving multiple minor GCs.
questions.explanation: When medium-lived objects survive minor collections (Scavenge) repeatedly, they get promoted to the old generation space. If many such objects accumulate and eventually die, they leave memory fragmentation and trigger expensive major Mark-Sweep-Compact cycles even if total heap size stays relatively flat.
questions.hint: Think about the lifecycle of objects traversing between the young and old generations.
questions.relatedConcept: V8 Garbage Collection Generations and Promotion Dynamics
questions.interviewTip: This tests advanced performance debugging skills, distinguishing between out-of-memory leaks and generational heap churn.

title: TypeScript - Test 1: Core Fundamentals & Patterns
description: Comprehensive technical evaluation for TypeScript covering runtime mechanics, design principles, and problem solving.

questions.question: [TypeScript • Test 1 • Q1] Why do database storage engines (InnoDB, Postgres) utilize B+ Trees instead of standard Binary Search Trees?
options: B+ Trees eliminate all disk writes.
Binary trees cannot store string keys.
B+ Trees automatically compress data in RAM.
High fan-out minimizes disk I/O depth (O(log_B N)), and linked leaf nodes allow sequential range scans.
questions.correctAnswer: High fan-out minimizes disk I/O depth (O(log_B N)), and linked leaf nodes allow sequential range scans.
questions.explanation: B+ Trees store records only in linked leaves. The wide branching factor (high fan-out) reduces tree height to 3-4 levels for millions of rows.
questions.hint: High fan-out reduces disk page reads.
questions.relatedConcept: TypeScript - B+ Tree Indexing & Range Lookups
questions.interviewTip: Understand covering index (index-only scan) optimization for SQL queries.

questions.question: [TypeScript • Test 1 • Q2] What is the primary purpose of the Circuit Breaker pattern in microservice architecture?
options: Encrypts payload traffic with TLS.
Fails fast when downstream services become unresponsive, preventing cascading thread starvation across the system.
Balances network load across all containers.
Compresses JSON responses.
questions.correctAnswer: Fails fast when downstream services become unresponsive, preventing cascading thread starvation across the system.
questions.explanation: Circuit Breakers track failure rates and trip Open to reject requests immediately, returning fallback responses until health recovers.
questions.hint: Fails fast to protect system resilience.
questions.relatedConcept: TypeScript - Microservices Circuit Breaker Pattern
questions.interviewTip: Always define fallbacks and reasonable timeout thresholds for HTTP clients.

questions.question: [TypeScript • Test 1 • Q3] What causes Thrashing in Operating System memory management?
options: CPU clock speed throttled due to temperature.
Network sockets buffer overflow.
Deadlock among mutual exclusion locks.
Main memory is overloaded, causing the OS to spend more time swapping pages to disk than executing process instructions.
questions.correctAnswer: Main memory is overloaded, causing the OS to spend more time swapping pages to disk than executing process instructions.
questions.explanation: Thrashing occurs when active working sets exceed physical RAM, causing continuous page faults and disk I/O thrashing.
questions.hint: Continuous page faults and disk swapping.
questions.relatedConcept: TypeScript - OS Virtual Memory & Page Replacement
questions.interviewTip: Working set model prevents thrashing by ensuring processes have sufficient page frames.

questions.question: [TypeScript • Test 1 • Q4] What is the sequence of control flags exchanged during the standard TCP connection establishment?
options: ACK -> SYN -> FIN
SYN -> SYN-ACK -> ACK
SYN -> ACK -> DATA
RST -> SYN -> ACK
questions.correctAnswer: SYN -> SYN-ACK -> ACK
questions.explanation: Client sends SYN with initial sequence number (ISN), Server responds with SYN-ACK, Client sends ACK to establish full-duplex session.
questions.hint: Synchronize, Synchronize-Acknowledge, Acknowledge.
questions.relatedConcept: TypeScript - TCP 3-Way Handshake & Flow Control
questions.interviewTip: TCP 3-way handshake sequence is a universal computer network interview question.

questions.question: [TypeScript • Test 1 • Q5] In SOLID principles, what does the Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP) enforce?
options: Every class must inherit from exactly one parent.
Classes should be open for modification and closed for extension.
Dependencies must be hardcoded statically.
Objects of a superclass should be replaceable with objects of its subclasses without altering program correctness.
questions.correctAnswer: Objects of a superclass should be replaceable with objects of its subclasses without altering program correctness.
questions.explanation: LSP guarantees that derived classes honor the contract and behavior expectations established by the base type.
questions.hint: Subtypes must be substitutable for their base types.
questions.relatedConcept: TypeScript - Object Oriented Design & SOLID Principles
questions.interviewTip: Violating LSP often occurs when overriding methods with empty implementations or unexpected exceptions.

questions.question: [TypeScript • Test 1 • Q6] In Distributed Storage, how does Consistent Hashing minimize partition migration when a node is added?
options: Rehashes all keys across all servers from scratch.
Maps servers and keys to a 360-degree hash ring, so adding a node only migrates k/N keys from its immediate neighbor.
Duplicates all partitions to every machine in cluster.
Freezes all transactions until rebalancing completes.
questions.correctAnswer: Maps servers and keys to a 360-degree hash ring, so adding a node only migrates k/N keys from its immediate neighbor.
questions.explanation: Consistent Hashing ensures that only adjacent ring segments are redistributed, minimizing network transfer during cluster scaling.
questions.hint: Hash ring bounds key migration to immediate neighbors.
questions.relatedConcept: TypeScript - Consistent Hashing in Distributed Systems
questions.interviewTip: Amazon DynamoDB and Cassandra use consistent hashing with virtual nodes.

questions.question: [TypeScript • Test 1 • Q7] Which SQL transaction isolation level prevents Dirty Reads and Non-Repeatable Reads, but may allow Phantom Reads?
options: READ COMMITTED
READ UNCOMMITTED
SERIALIZABLE
REPEATABLE READ
questions.correctAnswer: REPEATABLE READ
questions.explanation: Repeatable Read locks scanned rows preventing updates, but standard SQL allows concurrent transactions to insert new matching rows (phantoms).
questions.hint: Read Uncommitted < Read Committed < Repeatable Read < Serializable.
questions.relatedConcept: TypeScript - ACID Isolation & Concurrency Anomalies
questions.interviewTip: Serializable eliminates all anomalies via strict range locking or SSI.

questions.question: [TypeScript • Test 1 • Q8] What is the exact compile-time behavior of TypeScript's `const` assertions when applied to object and array literals?
questions.codeSnippet:
const config = { endpoint: '/api/v1', retries: 3 } as const;
// What is the resulting type of config?
options: Properties are marked as readonly, and literal values are widened to primitive types like string and number.
Properties are deeply marked as readonly, and literal values are narrowed to exact singleton literal types rather than widened.
Properties are mutable, but their types become exact string and numeric literal types.
Properties are treated as optional and typed as `any` to allow flexible configuration overriding.
questions.correctAnswer: Properties are deeply marked as readonly, and literal values are narrowed to exact singleton literal types rather than widened.
questions.explanation: A `const` assertion (`as const`) tells the TypeScript compiler to infer the most specific narrow type for an expression, recursively turning object properties into `readonly` and converting primitive literals into exact singleton literal types (e.g., `'/api/v1'` instead of `string`).
questions.hint: Think about how literal widening is prevented and what happens to mutability recursively.
questions.relatedConcept: TypeScript Const Assertions & Literal Narrowing
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to verify whether candidates understand immutability and literal type preservation beyond standard `const` variable declarations.

questions.question: [TypeScript • Test 1 • Q9] How does TypeScript's structural type system treat excess properties when an object literal is directly assigned to a function parameter compared to when it is assigned via an intermediate variable?
options: Both Case A and Case B trigger compilation errors because of unexpected property 'z'.
Both Case A and Case B succeed silently by stripping property 'z' at runtime.
Case A triggers an excess property error, whereas Case B succeeds due to duck typing and object reference assignment.
Case A succeeds via type widening, whereas Case B triggers an excess property error.
questions.correctAnswer: Case A triggers an excess property error, whereas Case B succeeds due to duck typing and object reference assignment.
questions.explanation: TypeScript performs Excess Property Checks specifically on fresh object literals (Case A) to catch common typos. When assigned through an intermediate variable (Case B), the freshness is lost, and standard structural subtyping rules apply, allowing extra properties as long as the mandatory ones are present.
questions.hint: Consider the concept of 'freshness' in object literal assignments versus variable references.
questions.relatedConcept: TypeScript Excess Property Checks & Structural Typing
questions.interviewTip: This is a classic distinction that separates intermediate TypeScript developers from those who truly understand the compiler's safety heuristics.

questions.question: [TypeScript • Test 1 • Q10] Given the TypeScript code below, which statement will cause a compile‑time error under the default `--strict` settings?
options: const p1: Person = { name: "Alice", age: 30, address: "123 Main St" };
const p3 = { name: "Carol", age: 28, extra: true };
const p4: Person = p3;
const p2: Person = { name: "Bob", age: 25, extra: true };
questions.correctAnswer: const p2: Person = { name: "Bob", age: 25, extra: true };
questions.explanation: Only the assignment to `p2` triggers an excess‑property check because the right‑hand side is an object literal containing the extra property `extra`. Excess property checks are applied only to object literals, not to variables like `p3`, so `p4` is allowed.
questions.hint: Recall when TypeScript performs excess‑property checking.
questions.relatedConcept: Excess Property Checks
questions.interviewTip: Shows the candidate understands structural typing and the subtle difference between literal assignment and variable assignment.

questions.question: [TypeScript • Test 1 • Q11] Given an array of user objects and a Map that indexes the same users by their ID, which lookup method has the lowest average‑case time complexity?
options: Map.get – O(1) average‑case lookup
Array.find – O(n) linear search
Both are O(1) because V8 optimises array lookups
Both are O(n) because the Map still iterates internally
questions.correctAnswer: Map.get – O(1) average‑case lookup
questions.explanation: Map.get performs a hash‑table lookup, which is O(1) on average. Array.find iterates until it finds a matching element, giving O(n) in the worst and average case. The other options misstate V8's behaviour.
questions.hint: Think about how each data structure is accessed internally.
questions.relatedConcept: Data‑structure lookup complexity in TypeScript/JavaScript (Array vs Map)
questions.interviewTip: Shows whether the candidate knows when to prefer hash‑based collections over linear scans for performance.

questions.question: [TypeScript • Test 1 • Q12] Which of the following shallow‑clone techniques is generally the most performant for a plain object with many enumerable own properties?
options: Object.assign({}, source)
Manual for‑in loop copying each property
Spread syntax: {...source}
JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(source))
questions.correctAnswer: Manual for‑in loop copying each property
questions.explanation: A manual for‑in loop avoids the overhead of function calls and internal bookkeeping that Object.assign and spread incur, making it the fastest for a pure shallow copy. JSON serialization is the slowest due to string conversion.
questions.hint: Consider the cost of extra function calls versus a straight loop.
questions.relatedConcept: Runtime cost of object cloning patterns in TypeScript/JavaScript
questions.interviewTip: Helps assess the candidate’s awareness of practical performance trade‑offs beyond just syntax convenience.

options: The function will throw a runtime error if called.
TypeScript will infer a more specific type automatically.
Callers cannot rely on the shape of the returned object, reducing type safety.
The function must be declared 'async' to return 'any'.
questions.correctAnswer: Callers cannot rely on the shape of the returned object, reducing type safety.
questions.explanation: Declaring a function return type as `any` disables compile‑time type checking for callers; the shape of the returned object is unknown, which defeats one of TypeScript’s main benefits. The other options are incorrect because the function will still execute normally, TypeScript does not automatically narrow the type, and `any` can be used with both sync and async functions.
questions.hint: Think about what the compiler can verify when the return type is `any`.
questions.relatedConcept: TypeScript type safety and the dangers of using `any`
questions.interviewTip: Reviewers look for any usage of `any` that could be replaced with a proper interface or type alias to maintain type safety.

questions.question: [TypeScript • Test 1 • Q15] In TypeScript you use a WeakMap to cache expensive results keyed by object instances. Which statement best describes the memory behavior of the WeakMap entries?
options: The key object is held weakly; if no other strong references exist elsewhere, the entry can be garbage collected automatically.
The key object is strongly referenced, preventing it from being garbage collected until the WeakMap itself is cleared.
The entry remains in memory forever because WeakMap entries are never removed.
The value is also held weakly, so both key and value can be collected simultaneously.
questions.correctAnswer: The key object is held weakly; if no other strong references exist elsewhere, the entry can be garbage collected automatically.
questions.explanation: WeakMap keys are weakly referenced; when no other strong references to the key exist, the entire entry is eligible for garbage collection. Values are still strongly referenced only while the key exists. The other options incorrectly state strong key reference, eternal retention, or weak values.
questions.hint: Think about what ‘weak’ means for the key.
questions.relatedConcept: WeakMap key references and garbage collection
questions.interviewTip: Tests knowledge of how WeakMap prevents memory leaks in caching patterns.

questions.question: [TypeScript • Test 1 • Q17] What is the primary compilation and runtime behavior of TypeScript enum members when declared with the `const` modifier?
options: They generate a JavaScript object with bidirectional mappings at runtime just like regular enums.
They throw a compilation error unless isolatedModules is explicitly set to false.
They are completely inlined at usage sites during compilation, leaving no runtime object representation.
They are evaluated lazily at runtime the first time the enum member is accessed.
questions.correctAnswer: They are completely inlined at usage sites during compilation, leaving no runtime object representation.
questions.explanation: Const enums in TypeScript do not emit any JavaScript object or runtime code for the enum itself. Instead, the TypeScript compiler performs inlining, replacing any reference to a const enum member with its evaluated numeric or string literal value directly in the generated JavaScript.
questions.hint: Think about what happens to the output JavaScript file size and structure when using 'const enum' vs standard enum.
questions.relatedConcept: TypeScript - Const Enums Inlining and Compilation Output
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to check if candidates understand the distinction between TypeScript's type-level abstractions and emission-level code generation.

questions.question: [TypeScript • Test 1 • Q18] How does TypeScript's conditional type distribution behave when applied to a naked type parameter versus a wrapped type parameter?
questions.codeSnippet:
type ToArray<T> = T extends any ? T[] : never;
type Result = ToArray<string | number>;
options: It evaluates the union as a single entity, resulting in (string | number)[].
It triggers a circular type reference compilation error.
It evaluates to never because string and number do not extend any.
It distributes over union types, resulting in string[] | number[].
questions.correctAnswer: It distributes over union types, resulting in string[] | number[].
questions.explanation: When conditional types act on a generic type parameter that is naked (unwrapped, i.e., T extends ...), they automatically distribute over union types. Thus, ToArray<string | number> becomes ToArray<string> | ToArray<number>, yielding string[] | number[].
questions.hint: Look closely at whether the type parameter on the left side of 'extends' is wrapped in a tuple or array.
questions.relatedConcept: TypeScript - Distributive Conditional Types
questions.interviewTip: This question tests advanced type system mastery, particularly how TypeScript handles union expansion in conditional types.

questions.question: [TypeScript • Test 1 • Q19] What does a TypeScript compilation error stating 'Property 'foo' does not exist on type 'unknown'' fundamentally imply about the safety rules enforced by the compiler?
questions.codeSnippet:
let val: unknown = getData();
console.log(val.foo);
options: The compiler forces explicit type narrowing or type assertions before allowing property access on 'unknown' to ensure runtime safety.
The variable 'val' has been inferred as 'any', but strict null checks prevent property access.
The type 'unknown' automatically strips all properties during compilation, turning the object into a primitive.
The compiler has optimized away the object reference because its shape cannot be statically verified at compile time.
questions.correctAnswer: The compiler forces explicit type narrowing or type assertions before allowing property access on 'unknown' to ensure runtime safety.
questions.explanation: The 'unknown' type is TypeScript's type-safe counterpart to 'any'. Unlike 'any', the compiler prevents any operations (such as property access, method calls, or function execution) on values of type 'unknown' until the developer performs a type check or type assertion.
questions.hint: Think about how 'unknown' differs from 'any' regarding immediate operability.
questions.relatedConcept: TypeScript - Type Safety and the 'unknown' Type Semantics
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to test if candidates understand how TypeScript achieves type safety without completely abandoning flexibility.

questions.question: [TypeScript • Test 1 • Q20] When TypeScript issues the error 'Type instantiation is excessively deep and possibly infinite', what underlying compiler mechanism has been tripped?
questions.codeSnippet: type DeepRecursive<T> = DeepRecursive<{ nested: T }>;
options: The JavaScript runtime has run out of stack space due to infinite tail-call recursion in generic functions.
The TypeScript type checker's recursion depth limit for conditional or mapped types has been exceeded.
The module bundler has encountered a cyclic dependency loop during AST generation.
The TypeScript compiler's garbage collector has failed to free memory allocated for structural subtyping.
questions.correctAnswer: The TypeScript type checker's recursion depth limit for conditional or mapped types has been exceeded.
questions.explanation: TypeScript enforces an internal recursion depth limit when evaluating complex conditional types, recursive type aliases, or heavily nested generic instantiations to prevent compiler lockups or infinite loops during type checking.
questions.hint: This error occurs entirely within the compiler during type analysis, not at runtime.
questions.relatedConcept: TypeScript - Recursive Type Depth Limits and Compiler Diagnostics
questions.interviewTip: This question screens for advanced TypeScript experience involving complex type-level programming and conditional type utilities.

questions.question: [TypeScript • Test 1 • Q21] What is the structural behavior and type inference outcome of using a Template Literal Type that maps over a union containing `any` or `never` in TypeScript?
questions.codeSnippet:
type Prefix<T extends string> = `get_${T}`;
type Result = Prefix<string | never>;
options: Result resolves to `never` because the presence of `never` in a union short-circuits distributive conditional types.
Result resolves to `any` because string templates with unconstrained primitives widen to `any`.
Result resolves to `get_${string}` because `never` distributes out and is ignored while `string` is preserved.
TypeScript throws a compilation error due to mixing distributive types with template literal widenings.
questions.correctAnswer: Result resolves to `get_${string}` because `never` distributes out and is ignored while `string` is preserved.
questions.explanation: In TypeScript, when a template literal type is applied to a union that includes `never`, `never` is effectively ignored during distribution since it represents the empty set. Applying it to `string` yields `get_${string}`.
questions.hint: Consider how union distribution handles the empty type `never` versus the wildcard type `string`.
questions.relatedConcept: Template Literal Types & Union Distribution
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use advanced type system nuances like template literal distribution to test if candidates understand type-level set theory.

questions.question: [TypeScript • Test 1 • Q22] How does TypeScript handle type narrowing when encountering a user-defined type guard that returns a signature using `asserts` instead of a boolean?
options: The variable `x` remains `string | number` unless assigned explicitly, because assertion signatures only alter return types, not local scope bindings.
TypeScript produces a compile-time error because `asserts` signatures cannot be used on union types.
The variable `x` is narrowed to `never` because the compiler treats any custom assertion function as an unhandled side effect.
The variable `x` is narrowed to `string` in the current scope because an assertion function throws on failure, allowing the control flow analyzer to assume success post-call.
questions.correctAnswer: The variable `x` is narrowed to `string` in the current scope because an assertion function throws on failure, allowing the control flow analyzer to assume success post-call.
questions.explanation: Assertion signatures (`asserts val is T`) inform the TypeScript control flow analysis that if the function returns normally without throwing, the tested variable must satisfy type `T` for the remainder of the scope.
questions.hint: Think about what control flow analysis assumes when a function completes successfully without throwing an error.
questions.relatedConcept: Assertion Signatures & Control Flow Narrowing
questions.interviewTip: Useful for verifying if the candidate knows modern TypeScript control flow features beyond basic `typeof` checks.

questions.question: [TypeScript • Test 1 • Q23] What is the primary difference in behavior between TypeScript's `ReturnType<T>` utility type and manually declaring a return type extraction when `T` represents an overloaded function?
options: ReturnType extracts the return type of the first overload signature defined in the function.
ReturnType only inspects the last signature overload defined in the function implementation.
ReturnType distributes over union types and returns a union of all possible overload return types.
ReturnType returns the return type of the implementation signature rather than the overload signatures.
questions.correctAnswer: ReturnType only inspects the last signature overload defined in the function implementation.
questions.explanation: In TypeScript, conditional types and utility types like ReturnType that infer from function types only inspect the *last* signature overload in the list of overloads, ignoring any preceding overloads.
questions.hint: Think about how conditional type inference behaves when encountering multiple function overloads.
questions.relatedConcept: TypeScript Function Overload Inference Limitations
questions.interviewTip: Use this to test deep knowledge of TypeScript's type system limitations regarding function overloads.

questions.question: [TypeScript • Test 1 • Q24] How does TypeScript handle type checking for an empty object literal assigned to a type that has all optional properties?
options: It triggers a compilation error because empty object literals are subject to excess property checks.
It is disallowed unless the type explicitly includes an index signature [key: string]: unknown.
It is allowed because all properties are optional, so an empty object satisfies the shape structurally.
It raises a warning in strict mode but compiles successfully otherwise.
questions.correctAnswer: It is allowed because all properties are optional, so an empty object satisfies the shape structurally.
questions.explanation: An empty object literal {} is completely compatible with an interface where all properties are optional because structural subtyping allows missing optional properties without triggering excess property checks (excess property checks only apply to fresh object literals containing properties not found in the target type).
questions.hint: Consider whether excess property checks trigger when no properties are provided at all.
questions.relatedConcept: TypeScript Structural Typing with Optional Properties
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to check if candidates understand the nuance between excess property checks and standard structural subtyping.

questions.question: [TypeScript • Test 1 • Q25] What happens when you apply the `keyof` operator to a type that has a numeric index signature in TypeScript?
options: Keys evaluates to type `string`.
Keys evaluates to `number | string`.
TypeScript throws a compilation error because index signatures cannot be used with keyof.
Keys evaluates to type `number`.
questions.correctAnswer: Keys evaluates to type `number`.
questions.explanation: In TypeScript, when an interface or type has a numeric index signature, the `keyof` operator evaluates to `number` (and similarly, a string index signature evaluates to `string | number` because JavaScript object keys are coerced to strings, but specifically numeric index signatures yield `number`).
questions.hint: Think about what type JavaScript uses to index arrays or objects with numeric keys.
questions.relatedConcept: Numeric index signatures and keyof operator behavior
questions.interviewTip: Intervers use this to test your understanding of type-level operators and how JavaScript's runtime behavior maps to TypeScript's type system.

questions.question: [TypeScript • Test 1 • Q26] Consider the following TypeScript code utilizing conditional types and deferred type checking. What is the precise reason TypeScript throws a compilation error on this snippet?
options: The return type `Unwrap<T>` is a conditional type that depends on the generic type parameter `T`, making it non-distributive or unconstrained, so the compiler cannot guarantee that `val` (of type `T`) is assignable to `Unwrap<T>` prior to instantiation.
The `infer` keyword cannot be used inside functions, only within type alias declarations.
Conditional types are evaluated only at runtime and cannot be used as function return annotations.
The variable `val` must be explicitly cast to `any` before it can be returned from a function with a conditional return type.
questions.correctAnswer: The return type `Unwrap<T>` is a conditional type that depends on the generic type parameter `T`, making it non-distributive or unconstrained, so the compiler cannot guarantee that `val` (of type `T`) is assignable to `Unwrap<T>` prior to instantiation.
questions.explanation: TypeScript considers conditional types whose checked type is a generic parameter (like `T extends ...`) to be dependent on that generic type. Because the compiler cannot verify that the generic type `T` is unconditionally assignable to the conditional return type `Unwrap<T>` for all possible instantiations of `T`, it flags a type safety error until a type assertion or constraint is applied.
questions.hint: Focus on why the compiler cannot prove assignability of an unconstrained generic type to a conditional type.
questions.relatedConcept: Generic conditional type assignability checks
questions.interviewTip: This tests deep familiarity with TypeScript's type checker limitations regarding generic conditional types and function return type verification.

questions.question: [TypeScript • Test 1 • Q27] What is the primary runtime memory and performance trade-off of utilizing TypeScript 'enum' constructs compared to 'const enum' when compiled to standard JavaScript (ES5/ES6)?
questions.codeSnippet: enum Direction { Up, Down }\nconst enum Status { Active, Inactive }
options: Standard enums are optimized away by the TypeScript compiler into primitive numbers, while const enums require an external polyfill library to execute safely.

Standard enums generate bidirectional object maps at runtime, increasing bundle size and adding property lookup overhead, whereas const enums are completely inlined at usage sites leaving zero runtime artifacts.
Standard enums execute entirely on the type-checker level with no output, while const enums create heavy prototype inheritance chains at runtime.
Both standard and const enums generate identical IIFE objects at runtime, making their performance impact indistinguishable in modern V8 engines.
questions.correctAnswer: Standard enums generate bidirectional object maps at runtime, increasing bundle size and adding property lookup overhead, whereas const enums are completely inlined at usage sites leaving zero runtime artifacts.
questions.explanation: Standard TypeScript enums produce a physical JavaScript object mapping names to values and values to names (for reverse mapping), consuming memory and adding property lookups. Const enums are stripped entirely during compilation, replacing references directly with their literal values.
questions.hint: Consider how the compiler translates enum objects versus how it handles const declarations during lowering.
questions.relatedConcept: TypeScript Enum Compilation Overhead & Inlining Optimization
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to test whether developers understand the distinction between TypeScript's type-level abstractions and their actual generated JavaScript runtime footprints.

questions.question: [TypeScript • Test 1 • Q28] When leveraging TypeScript conditional types with distributive behavior over union types, what is the primary performance and complexity trap to avoid in large-scale type definitions?
questions.codeSnippet: type Distributive<T> = T extends any ? Wrapper<T> : never;
options: Distributive conditional types disable all structural subtyping checks, leading to silent memory leaks in the V8 garbage collector during runtime execution.
Distributive conditional types force the TypeScript compiler to convert all union types into intersections, causing infinite recursion errors at runtime.

Distributive conditional types automatically trigger exponential type-checking instantiation and combinatorial explosion when evaluated over large union types, drastically slowing down IDE language server responsiveness.
Distributive conditional types prevent tree-shaking of unused modules during the Webpack or Vite bundling phase.
questions.correctAnswer: Distributive conditional types automatically trigger exponential type-checking instantiation and combinatorial explosion when evaluated over large union types, drastically slowing down IDE language server responsiveness.
questions.explanation: When a conditional type is distributive, TypeScript evaluates each member of the union separately. If fed a large union (e.g., unions of keys or nested structures), this creates a combinatorial explosion in instantiation paths, heavily impacting TypeScript compiler (tsc) performance.
questions.hint: Think about how TypeScript evaluates type aliases over massive union sets and the impact on the compiler's type instantiation pool.
questions.relatedConcept: TypeScript Type-Checking Complexity & Combinatorial Union Explosion
questions.interviewTip: Senior engineers are often asked this to demonstrate awareness of compile-time performance bottlenecks in enterprise monorepos with heavy type-level programming.

questions.question: [TypeScript • Test 1 • Q29] When a reviewer flags the use of TypeScript's 'any' type in a strict codebase, which idiomatic feature should they typically recommend as a type-safe alternative for values whose type is unknown at write-time?
options: never
void
Record<string, object>
unknown
questions.correctAnswer: unknown
questions.explanation: The 'unknown' type is the type-safe counterpart to 'any'. While anything is assignable to 'unknown', 'unknown' is not assignable to anything except itself and 'any' without performing a type narrowing check, preventing unsafe operations.
questions.hint: Think of the type that forces you to prove or narrow the type before you can call methods on it.
questions.relatedConcept: TypeScript type safety vs 'any' escape hatches
questions.interviewTip: Interweaves idiomatic code review standards with type-level mechanics.

questions.question: [TypeScript • Test 1 • Q30] What code review concern does an idiomatic TypeScript linter flag when it encounters a non-null assertion operator ('!') placed at the end of a method chain?
questions.codeSnippet: const length = user.getProfile()!.settings!.theme!.length;
options: It suppresses TypeScript's null-safety checks and can easily cause runtime TypeError crashes if any intermediate link is undefined.
It triggers an automatic boxing performance penalty because primitives are converted to wrapper objects.
It creates a circular module dependency warning during the compilation phase.
It forces the TypeScript compiler to downgrade the target ES version to ES5.
questions.correctAnswer: It suppresses TypeScript's null-safety checks and can easily cause runtime TypeError crashes if any intermediate link is undefined.
questions.explanation: The non-null assertion operator (!) blindly tells the compiler to trust that a value is neither null nor undefined. If an intermediate property turns out to be undefined at runtime, the application will throw a TypeError, undermining TypeScript's safety guarantees.
questions.hint: Consider what the '!' operator instructs the compiler to ignore.
questions.relatedConcept: TypeScript Non-null Assertion Operator anti-patterns
questions.interviewTip: Evaluates a candidate's practical intuition regarding defensive coding and type assertions.

questions.question: [Go • Test 1 • Q1] What is the exact execution behavior of the following Go code snippet involving deferred function evaluation and named return values?
options: Compilation error: cannot modify named return value inside literal defer
